query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: When HEA nanoparticles are synthesized under conditions that restrict atomic mobility (for example, via low‐temperature reduction from a single‐source precursor), the resulting kinetically frozen, near-equiatomic solid solution is stabilized by suppressed precursor diffusion. This limited mobility minimizes elemental segregation and phase separation during subsequent thermal exposure (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use), even when noble metal content is low.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles formed from single‐source precursors using low-temperature or rapid cooling processes that inhibit atomic diffusion.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled post-synthesis annealing step to deliberately increase the free atom mobility (for instance, a brief hold at a moderately elevated temperature below service regime) compared to a baseline where mobility remains inhibited.
generation.conditions: The nanoparticles are evaluated under high-temperature operating conditions (catalytic operation at 773–1173 K or thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K). The controlled intervention is applied prior to subjecting the samples to these service temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The key mediator is the degree of atomic mobility (or diffusion) during and immediately after synthesis, which governs the formation of a random solid solution and anchors elements into a single-phase lattice.
generation.mechanism: Limited atomic mobility during synthesis freezes a high-entropy, random alloy configuration, thereby suppressing thermodynamically driven phase separation or segregation during service. In contrast, increased mobility—via a controlled annealing step—allows atoms to rearrange, thereby enhancing local segregation and the eventual formation of secondary phases under service conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized with inhibited atomic mobility will display uniform elemental distribution and retain a single-phase structure upon high-temperature exposure. In contrast, those subjected to the post-synthesis mobility-enhancing anneal will show evidence of elemental segregation, increased lattice strain, and the emergence of secondary phases, leading to reduced catalytic or thermoelectric performance relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: HEA nanoparticles synthesized by low-temperature reduction with restricted atom mobility without any additional annealing intervention.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for nanoparticles produced from chemically mixed single‐source precursors under synthesis conditions where free atom mobility is naturally limited (e.g., solid-state or rapid-cooling processes) and evaluated in service regimes at temperatures typical for catalysis (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric applications (473–1923 K). It may not directly apply to solution-based syntheses where atomic mobility is inherently higher.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative thresholds of 'limited' atomic mobility and the precise thermal budgets that might trigger segregation are not yet defined. Also, the interplay with support interactions or surface effects was not explored in detail.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles under identical precursor conditions. Set A is synthesized via the standard low-temperature reduction method to restrict atomic mobility, while set B is subjected to an additional controlled annealing step designed to enhance atomic diffusion (without altering composition). Both sets are then exposed to service-like temperatures (e.g., 800 K for catalytic conditions) for an extended period. Structural characterization (using in situ XRD, TEM, and elemental mapping) and performance tests (e.g., catalytic reaction yield) are conducted before and after the thermal exposure.
measurements: Elemental distribution homogeneity (via EDX mapping and atom probe tomography)
Phase identification (XRD and TEM diffraction patterns)
Lattice strain and defect analysis (via HAADF-STEM)
Catalytic or thermoelectric performance metrics compared to baseline
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles from set A (with limited mobility) exhibit similar levels of elemental segregation, phase separation, or performance degradation as seen in set B (annealed sample) upon high-temperature exposure, then the hypothesis that restricted atomic mobility stabilizes the single-phase structure is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways.
